profile.name: Alessio Iodice
profile.title: Software Engineer
profile.bio: Software Engineer with 6 years of experience at Deloitte Digital, designing and building integrations for high-traffic B2C e-commerce platforms on Salesforce Commerce Cloud. I'm currently expanding beyond my usual stack, learning Python, FastAPI and Vue by building personal projects.
profile.philosophy: I'm interested in systems that stay correct under partial failure and remain simple to reason about years later — transactional boundaries, idempotency, graceful degradation when a dependency goes down. Most of my six years at Deloitte have been spent on the seams between systems: order pipelines, CRM synchronisation, payment webhooks, catalogue ingestion — the places where two systems disagree about what happened. Outside of work I'm using personal projects to push into stacks I don't touch professionally: Python and FastAPI, Vue, and most recently Astro and Zod for this site.

caseStudies.title: Decoupling order capture from a flaky OMS
caseStudies.context: A B2C commerce platform on Salesforce Commerce Cloud needed to export every placed order to a downstream Order Management System for fulfilment.
caseStudies.problem: Calling the OMS synchronously during checkout meant that any slowness or downtime on the OMS side directly threatened the checkout flow itself — the two systems' availability was coupled when it shouldn't have been.
caseStudies.approach: Rather than calling the OMS inline, order export was modelled as a transactional outbox: the order and an export record are written in the same transaction, and a separate process delivers export records to the OMS asynchronously, retrying independently of checkout.
caseStudies.decisions: The outbox pattern was chosen specifically to decouple order capture from delivery, so a slow or unavailable OMS can never block or fail a checkout — the trade-off accepted was eventual, not immediate, consistency between the storefront and the OMS.
caseStudies.result: Order capture and OMS delivery became independently reliable: checkout no longer depends on OMS availability, and the system guarantees eventual consistency even under partial failure of the downstream service.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: Decoupling the write from the delivery is often more valuable than making the delivery itself faster — it changes what can fail without taking checkout down with it.

caseStudies.title: Keeping checkout alive when the CRM isn't
caseStudies.context: Customer profile data needed to stay synchronised between the commerce platform and an external CRM, and be available fast enough to use during checkout.
caseStudies.problem: A synchronous, single-write dependency on the CRM meant that any CRM slowness or outage risked degrading or breaking checkout for every customer, even though CRM data wasn't strictly required to complete a purchase.
caseStudies.approach: CRM synchronisation was implemented as a dual-write with asynchronous reconciliation, backed by a read-through cache so checkout reads served from cache rather than calling the CRM directly on every request.
caseStudies.decisions: Explicit graceful degradation was built in: if the CRM is unreachable, checkout falls back to cached or default behaviour instead of failing, trading short-term data freshness for availability of the critical path.
caseStudies.result: Checkout remains available during CRM outages or slowdowns, with reconciliation catching up the two systems asynchronously once the CRM recovers.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: Not every dependency deserves the same availability guarantee as the path it sits next to — deciding what checkout can survive without was as important as the integration code itself.

caseStudies.title: Webhooks without head-of-line blocking
caseStudies.context: Payment gateways (Adyen, Stripe) notify the platform of payment events via webhooks, which need to be processed reliably without missing or misordering critical state changes.
caseStudies.problem: Processing each webhook fully inline, in the request that receives it, risks head-of-line blocking: a slow or failing handler for one event delays or drops the processing of the events queued behind it.
caseStudies.approach: Webhook handling was implemented with ack-on-receipt semantics — the endpoint acknowledges receipt immediately and hands the event off for processing separately, so the gateway is never kept waiting on internal processing time.
caseStudies.decisions: The target architecture specified an asynchronous processing pipeline with a dead-letter queue for events that fail processing, so failures are isolated and retryable instead of blocking the stream of incoming events.
caseStudies.result: Webhook ingestion no longer risks blocking on slow downstream processing, and failed events are captured in a dead-letter queue rather than silently lost or retried inline.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: Acknowledging receipt and processing are two different responsibilities with two different reliability requirements — conflating them into one synchronous step is what causes head-of-line blocking in the first place.
